fr:title.text: Progress on Pratt parsers: precedence levels and per-level fixity

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Progress on Pratt parsers: precedence levels and per-level fixity

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Status update following sss-00BY (single-level Pratt parsers) and sss-00BZ (open directions). The "precedence and fixity" item from sss-00BZ's section 1 is now implemented in src/Examples/PrecPrattRDLater.agda (commit 19baf5c), and witness-level test infrastructure has matured around it.

File: src/Examples/PrecPrattRDLater.agda. Concretely realises the stratified inductive grammar encoding from sss-00BZ's item 1: an indexed inductive E_p on a level p \in \mathrm {Fin}(\mathrm {suc}\,N) with

where \mathit {rhs}(q) is \mathrm {suc}\,q for right-associative levels and \mathsf {weakenFin}\,q for non-associative levels. The functor is F_E : \mathrm {Lev} \to \mathrm {Functor}\,\mathrm {Lev} and the grammar is \mu F_E.
Spec:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
data Fixity : Type ℓ-zero where rightAssoc nonAssoc : Fixity
record PrecPrattSpec : Type₁ where field N : ℕ -- number of operator levels AI : Type ℓ-zero -- atom token indices isSetAI : isSet AI O : Fin N → Type ℓ-zero -- operator indices per level isSetO : ∀ q → isSet (O q) fixity : Fin N → Fixity -- per-level fixity
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Alphabet: \mathrm {AI} \uplus (\Sigma \, q\, .\, O\,q). The per-level operator-index types are existentially packed into the alphabet so that the parser body can dispatch on a concrete pair (q', o') via \oplus ^\mathsf {d}\text {-elim} and then test q' \stackrel {?}{=} q with discreteFin.

fr:title.text: Per-level Löb fixpoint vs. direct call

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Per-level Löb fixpoint vs. direct call

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The parser body splits cleanly on fixity:

html:ul.html:li: rightAssoc (Step module). One \triangleright -fixpoint per level. The recursive call at a same-level op site consumes the runtime prefix E_{\mathsf {weakenFin}\,q} \otimes \mathsf {literal}\, (\mathit {op}) via \triangleright \text {-app-NE} with an inline prefix-NE proof — the literal contributes at least one character, so the consumed prefix is non-empty regardless of the LHS shape.

nonAssoc (Step-NA module). No fixpoint. After the operator, the RHS is at the tighter level and is parsed by calling the tighter parser directly. A second same-level op then falls through to the leftover, where the top-level runP rejects it. So a == b == c fails when == is non-assoc, exactly as desired.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Dispatch: parseAtLevel-suc q tighter branches on fixity q. To make the dispatch reduce at concrete specs, the fixity match is wrapped in go (fx : Fixity) → fixity q Eq.≡ fx → ..., applied to Eq.refl. At a fully-applied call site fixity q reduces to a constructor, the go pattern fires, and the body selects Step.step or Step-NA.step with a transported BINOP-o.

fr:title.text: Termination on ℕ rather than Fin

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Termination on ℕ rather than Fin

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The recursion parseAtLevel-aux is structured on n : \mathbb {N} with an external proof toℕ p ≡ n, not on the index p : \mathrm {Fin}(\mathrm {suc}\,N) itself. The reason is that weakenFin q is not structurally smaller than suc q in the FinData representation, so a direct recursion on p doesn't pass the termination checker. With n as the recursion variable and weakenRespToℕ closing the gap between toℕ (weakenFin q) and toℕ q, the proof is mechanical.

Each Build module exposes a Tree datatype mirroring the parse shape and a toTree algebra folding \mu F_E into Tree. The recogniser \mathsf {recognize\text {-}tree} : \mathrm {String} \to \mathsf {Maybe}\,\mathsf {Tree} materialises the tree, so tests can assert the actual parse shape rather than just acceptance.
Tests live in two files:

html:ul.html:li: PrecPrattRDLaterTests.agda — five tests with two levels: + at level 0, * at level 1, both right-assoc, exercising right-chains and precedence interleaving.
PrecPrattRDLaterMixedTests.agda — mixes a right-assoc level with a non-assoc level. Verifies the "fail on chain" behaviour for non-assoc operators.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Both files typecheck and all assertions go through by refl. The witness reduction is heavier than for a Bool acceptance test but tractable on the small (≤ 7-token) test inputs used.

fr:title.text: Companion development: witness performance and inspection

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Companion development: witness performance and inspection

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Three smaller commits since sss-00BY:

html:ul.html:li: fe6da88 — Eq-world variants of the ⌈⌉-⊗&-distL⁻/R⁻ witness lemmas. Stays in Cubical.Data.Equality rather than path equality when reasoning about splittings, which keeps hcomp from exploding witness reduction. This is the "two-tier opaque/transparent" idea from sss-00BZ's item 2, realised as a discipline rather than a marker.

066300a — parser-backed lex longest-match. Implements a Bool-oracle longest-prefix scan in Lex.Regex and Lex.Eval, using the regex parser from the Determinization pipeline. Adjacent to the parser work; the intent is to feed token streams into the Pratt parsers in a single end-to-end test.

716504a — PrattRDLaterNormalize scratch file for inspecting parser-witness normal forms inside an opaque unfolding eval-parser block. Development tool for the performance investigation from sss-00BZ's item 2.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The remaining items from sss-00BZ's item 1:

html:ul.html:li: Left-associativity per level or per operator. The current Fixity datatype has only rightAssoc and nonAssoc. Left-assoc requires either a loop-shaped recursion (accumulator-threaded \mathsf {fixP} at a residual carrier E \multimap \mathsf {Parser}\,E) or a post-process tree rotation that re-associates the right-spine output of the existing parser. The rotation route is straightforward but locally cosmetic; the loop route is the principled fix and gives left-assoc in the grammar denotation, not just in the tree.

Mixed-fixity at one level. Currently fixity is per level, which forces all operators sharing a precedence to agree on associativity. Realistic operator tables (e.g. + left-assoc and , right-assoc at the same precedence) would require per-operator fixity inside the same level — the Step/Step-NA dispatch generalises to per-op decRec, but the recursion shape would have to mix the two styles.

Unary prefix/postfix operators. Pratt parsers traditionally handle nud/led dispatch; the current framework is binary-only. Prefix is structurally easy (consume the op token then a level-p expression on the suffix); postfix needs the loop shape.

Ergonomic flat operator spec. The current PrecPrattSpec demands the user pre-stratify operators by level. A surface spec record FlatOp : (sym : Sym) (prec : ℕ) (fixity : Fixity) with a converter to PrecPrattSpec would make spec extension a one-line addition.

fr:title.text: Open directions for parser-combinators in dependent Lambek

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Open directions for parser-combinators in dependent Lambek

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Brainstorm capturing seven open directions for the parser combinator work tracked in sss-00BY. Each subtree is a short sketch — definitions, candidate approaches, and where they'd land in the existing library. Nothing here is implemented; each item is a starting point for a follow-up.

fr:title.text: 1. Pratt grammars parametric in precedence and fixity

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: 1. Pratt grammars parametric in precedence and fixity

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The generic parser in Examples.PrattRDLaterGen fixes one precedence level and right-associativity. To carry precedence p \in \{0, \dots , N\} and per-operator fixity, three viable encodings:

html:ul.html:li: Stratified inductive grammar. Index the grammar functor by precedence level: E_p := E_{p-1} \mid E_{p-1}\, op_p\, E_p (right-assoc) or with iteration for left-assoc. This is a mutually indexed inductive — define the functor F : \mathrm {Fin}\,N \to \mathrm {Functor}\,(\mathrm {Fin}\,N) and take \mu F. The parser becomes a finite tuple of mutually recursive Löb-fixed parsers, one per level.

Single grammar, precedence-indexed parser. Keep the grammar flat (E := A \mid A\, \mathrm {Op}\, E) and let the parser enforce precedence at parse time. Parser type: \mathrm {Lev} \to \mathsf {string} \vdash \mathsf {Parser}\,E. Löb-fix the whole family: \triangleright (\forall p.\,\mathsf {Parser}\,E) \vdash \forall p.\,\mathsf {Parser}\,E. This needs \triangleright to distribute through \Pi , which is standard in guarded type theory and should hold for the left-handed later modality in use here.

Per-operator threshold. Each operator carries (lbp, rbp). The parser checks \mathit {lbp}(\mathit {op}) > \mathrm {minPrec} and recurses with \mathit {rbp}(\mathit {op}). Right-assoc: \mathit {rbp} = \mathit {lbp} - 1; left-assoc: \mathit {rbp} = \mathit {lbp}. The left-assoc case requires the "loop" rather than "fold" recursion shape — see item 6 for the substring-modality angle.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Spec extension:
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
record OpInfo : Type where field prec : ℕ rightAssoc : Bool
record PrattSpec : Type₁ where field AI : Type ℓ-zero ; isSetAI : isSet AI OI : Type ℓ-zero ; isSetOI : isSet OI opInfo : OI → OpInfo
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The hard part isn't the spec — it's the parser body. The Löb-fixed precedence-indexed family is probably the cleanest path; the stratified inductive view is the cleanest grammar-level description.
The current tests assert acceptP w ≡ true via Bool-valued acceptance because building the full parse witness blows up term size. Sources of the blowup:

html:ul.html:li: Splittings: every \otimes carries a (w_1, w_2, p : w \equiv w_1 ++ w_2) record. Compositions stack these records.
Inductive grammar \mu F uses liftG/lowerG wrappers that don't reduce away under DSL combinators.
The Maybe⊗r, fmap, ⊕-elim chains produce nested case analyses that normalise to large terms even on small inputs.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Candidate fixes, roughly cheapest first:

html:ul.html:li: Bool-valued acceptance is sufficient most of the time. The current trick.

Structural test predicate. Define matchTree : Expr → BoolTree (a flat ADT mirroring the parse shape), recurse on the recognized witness, and compare against an expected BoolTree. This sidesteps splittings entirely. The "compare" reduces to Bool equality on a tree of tags.

Rewrite rules for monoidal laws. Declare \otimes -unit, \otimes -assoc, and \otimes -symmetry-equations as BUILTIN REWRITE, so that the elaborator collapses chains of ⊗-assoc⁻ ∘g ⊗-assoc during normalisation. Cubical paths complicate this — would need either eq-style rewrites (cf. AsEquality port) or careful `--rewriting` discipline.

Specialised evaluator. Write \mathsf {eval} : (\mathsf {string} \vdash \mathsf {Maybe}\,(A \otimes \mathsf {string})) \to \mathrm {List}\,\mathrm {Sym} \to \mathrm {Maybe}\,(\mathrm {AST}\,A \times \mathrm {List}\,\mathrm {Sym}) that interprets each DSL combinator on flat data structures (no splittings, no LiftG). Prove a correctness theorem once; then tests use eval for speed.

Two-tier opaque/transparent layers. The current eval-parser unfolds everything; consider a finer-grained eval-parser-tree marker that unfolds only the structural spine. The cubical paths in splittings would stay sealed.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The structural test predicate is probably the highest leverage — it captures the parse shape (which is what tests want to assert) without ever materialising splittings.
Two questions: can we do lexing in the DSL, and what's the ergonomic way to write test inputs.

In-DSL lexing. A lexer is a parser whose target grammar is a token stream. Building one in the DSL is mechanically possible: Kleene-*, \oplus , and disjunction are available. A LexerSpec record would carry per-token regexes plus a priority order (for longest-match / first-match disambiguation). Output: \mathsf {string}_\mathrm {raw} \vdash \mathsf {Maybe}\,(\mathrm {TokenList} \otimes \varepsilon ). The cost is non-trivial — whitespace handling, keyword tables, longest-match, error recovery — and offers no real benefit over an ordinary Agda function unless we want to reason semantically about lexer correctness in the same vocabulary as the parser.
Ergonomic test inputs. The pragmatic answer is to keep lexing external: an Agda function
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: lex : Agda.Builtin.String.String → List Sym lex s = lex' (primStringToList s) where lex' : List Char → List Sym lex' [] = [] lex' ('a' ∷ cs) = ⌜a⌝ ∷ lex' cs lex' ('+' ∷ cs) = ⌜+⌝ ∷ lex' cs ...
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Then acceptExpr (lex "a+b*a") typechecks and reduces identically to the hand-written a ∷ +t ∷ b ∷ *t ∷ a ∷ []. For multi-character tokens (let, =, identifiers), the lexer needs maximal-munch and a keyword table — also routine in plain Agda.

For the further-out goal of writing \texttt {"let x = 5 in x"} directly: combine the lexer above with a preprocessor that recognises identifiers and literals as token-with- payload. The token type extends from a plain enum to a tagged sum: Token = LET ∣ IN ∣ EQ ∣ IDENT String ∣ INT ℕ, and the parser's alphabet becomes this richer type (with appropriate isSet proof, e.g. via a retract through \mathbb {N} \uplus \mathrm {String} \uplus \mathrm {Fin}\,k).

Semantic bridging. If desired, prove \mathsf {lex}^* \equiv \mathsf {lex}_\mathrm {DSL} as a refinement theorem connecting the external lexer to an in-DSL specification. This pays for itself if you want end-to-end soundness statements ("parse of "a+b" produces this AST"), but isn't needed for the test-ergonomics use case alone.

The current type \mathsf {Parser}\,A = \mathsf {Maybe}\,(A \otimes \mathsf {string}) doesn't promise that nothing only fires on strings outside the language. A few ways to fix this in the type signature:

html:ul.html:li: Decision-procedure parsers. Replace the type with \mathsf {Parser}_!\,A = \mathsf {string} \cong (A \otimes \mathsf {string}) \oplus \mathrm {NoParse}_A where the right summand captures negative information ("no prefix of the input is in A"). NoParse is the tricky bit — it might be definable as \mathsf {string} \multimap (A \to \bot ) or via decidability witnesses.
Refinement-typed parsers. Bundle the morphism with its soundness/completeness proofs:
html:ul.html:pre: record CompleteParser (A : Grammar ℓ) : Type where field parse : string ⊢ Maybe (A ⊗ string) sound : ∀ w → parse w ≡ inl r → ⟨A w⟩ on (r.fst.fst) complete : ∀ w → parse w ≡ inr _ → ¬ ∃ accepting-split-of w
html:ul.html:li: Unambiguous-grammar route. For unambiguous LL(k) grammars, derive the parser directly from a grammar-equivalence proof \mathsf {string} \cong A \oplus \neg A. The Examples.BinOp.LL⟨1⟩ family already has this structure for LL(1); generalising the technique would be the principled route.
Total-by-construction. Index parsers by their language denotation; require that combinators preserve a "completeness" predicate (cf. item 5).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The cheapest practical move is the refinement-typed bundle — add soundness and completeness as ancillary fields that parser combinators thread through automatically. The unambiguous-grammar route is the most principled but requires a much heavier metatheory investment.
Danielsson's Total Parser Combinators (ICFP'10) builds total parsers in Agda by:

html:ol.html:li: Indexing parsers by the language they recognise (\mathsf {Parser}\,A\,L produces values of type A from inputs in L).
Encoding "consumes at least one token" as a type-level annotation (\mathit {null} vs \mathit {nonNull}) so that the combinator algebra rejects unproductive recursion.
Using coinductive/depth-indexed types so that the parser is total by construction.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Mapping to dependent Lambek:

html:ul.html:li: Language indexing is automatic — the grammar A is the language denotation, baked into the parser type.

Consumption annotation maps to the later modality: ▷-app-NE-keep-⌈⌉ requires a non-empty static prefix, which is exactly Danielsson's "must consume". So \triangleright on the left-handed modality corresponds to Danielsson's "delayed parser, productive after consumption".

Productivity / totality maps to Löb induction: the fixed-point combinator lob is well-defined precisely because every recursive call passes through \triangleright , mirroring how Danielsson's coinductive parsers are productive because every corecursive call passes through the depth annotation.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: So yes, the techniques apply, and the correspondence is reasonably tight: \triangleright \leftrightarrow consumption annotation, lob \leftrightarrow guarded fixed point, fixP \leftrightarrow fix on coinductive parsers. Direct adaptations worth importing:

html:ul.html:li: The "null"/"nonNull" distinction would let us forbid fixP id-style nonsense at the type level.

Danielsson's algebraic laws ((p₁ ⊕ p₂) ⊕ p₃ ≡ p₁ ⊕ (p₂ ⊕ p₃), left/right unit, etc.) transfer to our combinators essentially verbatim, and proving them would let combinator-level rewriting drive test-time normalisation (cf. item 2).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Current modalities: \triangleright (left-handed, consumes a non-empty prefix) and \triangleright ^r (right-handed, consumes a non-empty suffix). A natural third option is the substring modality \triangleright _\mathrm {sub}, expressing "later on any proper substring". sss-00B9 already sketches one shape for this; below fleshes out the elimination rule and the use case.
Semantic definition (on grammars):

i.e. there exists a decomposition w = u_1 \cdot w' \cdot u_2 with at least one of u_1, u_2 non-empty, and A holds on w'. (The two summands handle "left margin non-empty" and "right margin non-empty"; their overlap is also non-empty on both sides, which is fine since \oplus of A-witnesses is just "either witness".)
Elimination rule, by analogy with ▷-app-NE:

Fixed-point principle: \mathsf {lob}_\mathrm {sub} : (\triangleright _\mathrm {sub}\, A \vdash A) \to (\top \vdash A). Well-foundedness comes from |w'| < |w| whenever w = u_1 \cdot w' \cdot u_2 and one of u_1, u_2 is non-empty.

html:ul.html:li: Bracketed-content recursion without staging. Currently the parens parser consumes \langle , recurses on the suffix, then checks the inner leftover for \rangle . With \triangleright _\mathrm {sub}, we could directly recurse on "the content between \langle and \rangle " once we've found the matching close — a much more natural decomposition.

Dyck and similar grammars. The inner D in \langle D \rangle D is a proper substring of the outer input, not a suffix. With \triangleright _\mathrm {sub} we'd express this directly rather than via the suffix-and-leftover dance. See item 7.

Left-associative iteration. Reframe a left-assoc operator loop as: parse an atom a_n at the end of the input, recurse on the substring "everything before a_n" to get a_1 \, \mathit {op} \, \cdots \, \mathit {op} \, a_{n-1}. The recursive call is on a proper substring.
Two-sided patterns like a^n\, b\, c^n. The marker b is in the middle; recursion on the substring strictly between the two "ends" is the natural shape.

fr:title.text: 7. Dyck as a guarded fixed point

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: 7. Dyck as a guarded fixed point

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Cass's intuition (per discussion): the Dyck grammar can be described not just as the initial algebra \mu (I \oplus \langle \, X\, \rangle \, X) but as a guarded fixed point of a functor that turns "later grammars" into "current grammars" by consuming brackets.
Concretely:
The question marks are exactly the elimination of \triangleright _?: each occurrence of X is consumed at a position where the input has already given up at least one character. Two Xs appear:

html:ul.html:li: The inner X matches the contents between \langle and \rangle . Its input is a proper substring of the parent input (margins \langle and \rangle ++ \cdots on either side, both non-empty). Naturally a use of \triangleright _\mathrm {sub}.
The outer X matches the suffix after the closing \rangle . Its input is a proper suffix of the parent input. A use of \triangleright (left-handed).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: So the modality at the recursive position is a sort of join: either \triangleright or \triangleright _\mathrm {sub} suffices to witness productivity. One could take \triangleright _\mathrm {join} as the disjunction (a third modality), or use a heterogeneous functor where each X position is annotated with its own modality.

Connection to well-foundedness. The \mu -view of Dyck is the initial algebra of a polynomial functor; well-foundedness comes from structural induction on the inductive type. The guarded view gives an alternative justification: the unique fixed point under productivity. Both views coincide because Dyck is unambiguous — every Dyck word has exactly one parse tree.
Guarded fixed-point operator on grammars. The required primitive is

such that \mathsf {gfix}\, F \cong F(\mathrm {next}(\mathsf {gfix}\,F)) as grammars. This is the grammar-level analogue of lob (which operates at the term level on parser combinators). With it, Dyck = gfix DyckF, and we'd have a clean equivalence Dyck ≅ μ DyckBaseFunctor to relate the two encodings.

Payoff. Importing guarded-type-theory technology (clock variables, ticks, Iris-style modal reasoning) to grammars. Useful for: equivalences between \mu and \mathsf {gfix} definitions; modular productivity proofs that compose; semantic accounts of non-well-founded grammar definitions (e.g. infinite-arity \oplus _d where the index set itself is given by a guarded process).

fr:title.text: Recursive descent parsers in the dependent Lambek calculus

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Recursive descent parsers in the dependent Lambek calculus

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Notes on building small recursive descent parsers on top of the combinator library in Grammar.Parser, where recursion is encoded by Löb induction on the left-handed later modality \triangleright . Each parser is a closed term \mathtt {string} \vdash \mathsf {Maybe}\, A that reduces concretely on small inputs, so successful typechecking of refl-style tests is the evidence that the parser produces the right answer. Companion to sss-00BT (Chu / parser-combinator vocabulary) and to the ▷-modality construction in sss-00B9.

The DSL combinators (\otimes , \oplus , \triangleright -app, …) are mostly opaque, so reducing \mathtt {string} \vdash \mathsf {Maybe}\, A on a concrete word requires unfolding every primitive at the test site. Grammar.Parser.Eval bundles all the relevant unfoldings under a single marker eval-parser : Unit; a test file then writes
and inherits the entire chain transitively — Agda 2.9's unfolding is transitive through markers, so one local name buys access to dozens of opaques scattered across Grammar.*.
File: src/Examples/ArithRDLater.agda. Grammar

recognized by parseP = fixP step with step of type \triangleright A_0 \vdash A_0 dispatching on the first character of the input. The a-case consumes one character and recurses on the suffix via ▷-app-NE-keep-⌈⌉ aNE; the empty and +-cases emit NIL with the input left intact as leftover.

Tests in Examples/ArithRDLaterTests.agda: five refl-based assertions on a Bool-valued acceptAStr, mirroring the accept? trick from Examples/Benchmark/Dyck.agda. Witness-level reduction is expensive enough — even with all opaques unfolded — that we sidestep it pending a later performance investigation.
File: src/Examples/ArithParensRDLater.agda. Grammar

adding bracket tokens to the alphabet. The new open-bracket case projects \triangleright A_0 at the singleton prefix consisting of one open bracket, getting an inner parser result, then peeks at the inner leftover for a close bracket (via bindP) before constructing PARENSP. Inner failure or a missing close bracket both fail the whole branch.

Twelve refl-based acceptance tests in Examples/ArithParensRDLaterTests.agda cover nested parens, prefix-a^\ast sequences, and three failure cases (unmatched open, lone close, and trailing a after a closed group).
The simple template fixes a single static prefix per recursive call. Handling BinOp's grammar
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: E \;\;:=\;\; A \;\;\mid \;\; A + E, \qquad A \;\;:=\;\; n \;\;\mid \;\; \langle E \rangle
fr:mainmatter.html:p: from Examples.BinOp.LL⟨1⟩ bumps into this: after parsing a bracketed expression we would need to recurse again on a runtime-determined suffix to consume a possible + E, but ▷-app-NE-keep-⌈⌉ only projects \triangleright A_0 at a prefix we name statically. Two ways out:

html:ul.html:li: Duplicate \triangleright A_0 via the diagonal and use ▷-app-NE (the non-\lceil \cdot \rceil variant) with an ad-hoc NonEmpty proof for the bracketed prefix. Mechanically fine, but the proof obligation pollutes the parser body.

Use a different fixpoint shape that iterates rather than only recurses on the suffix. Pratt parsing is the canonical version: parseExp(minPrec) consumes an atom, then loops while the next operator's left binding power exceeds minPrec, with the operator's right binding power passed back into the recursive call. The loop body consumes a runtime-determined prefix per iteration (atom · op · atom · …), so the static-prefix restriction shows up as the central design problem rather than an asymmetry.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We take the second route below, but observe that the static-prefix restriction can be accommodated rather than overcome: every recursion site in a Pratt-style body consumes a 2-token prefix atom · op that is statically known after dispatching on those two tokens via \oplus ^\mathsf {d}-elim. The right-associative case becomes a one-pass Löb induction with prefix \lceil \mathit {atom}, \mathit {op} \rceil at each step.
File: src/Examples/PrattRDLater.agda. Grammar
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: E \;\;:=\;\; A \;\;\mid \;\; A + E, \qquad A \;\;:=\;\; a \;\;\mid \;\; \langle E \rangle
fr:mainmatter.html:p: with + right-associative. A single recursive parser via fixP. The body dispatches on the first character of the input:

html:ul.html:li: \langle : recurse to parse the inner E (project \triangleright A_0 at the singleton prefix \lceil \langle \rceil ), then peek the inner parser's leftover for \rangle via bindP, then build the PARENS node.

a: peek the next character. If it is +, project \triangleright A_0 at the two-character prefix \lceil a, +\rceil , parse the rhs E on the suffix, and combine into a PLUS node. Otherwise return the bare atom and leave whatever follows as the leftover.
anything else: fail.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The 2-character static prefix \lceil a, +\rceil gives every operator-recursion site a known static prefix atom-token · op-token, exactly the input shape that ▷-app-NE-keep-⌈⌉ can project. Eleven refl-based acceptance tests in Examples/PrattRDLaterTests.agda cover right-associated chains, paren groups, mixed sequences, and four failure cases (lone op, dangling op, op-leading, trailing atom).
File: src/Examples/PrattRDLaterGen.agda. A module Build parameterised by a record
fr:mainmatter.html:pre: record PrattSpec : Type₁ where field AI : Type ℓ-zero -- atom token indices isSetAI : isSet AI OI : Type ℓ-zero -- operator token indices isSetOI : isSet OI
fr:mainmatter.html:p: with alphabet \mathit {AI} \uplus \mathit {OI}. The grammar

has \mathsf {Atom} = \bigoplus _{a \in \mathit {AI}} \mathsf {literal}\,a and \mathsf {Op} = \bigoplus _{o \in \mathit {OI}} \mathsf {literal}\,o. The parser body dispatches on (i) the first character via the \uplus -structure of the alphabet, then (ii) inside the atom branch, on the second character. Each (atom, op) pair has its own static 2-token prefix, named uniformly in a, o.

Adding an operator is a one-line change to the OI datatype at the instantiation site — the parser body and proofs are untouched. Concrete tests in Examples/PrattRDLaterGenTests.agda instantiate with atoms \{a, b\} and operators \{+, *\}, ten refl-based assertions covering atom sequences, mixed-op chains, and failure cases.

fr:title.text: Where this stops: precedence and fixity

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Where this stops: precedence and fixity

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two extensions are still open:

html:ul.html:li: Multiple precedence levels. The current grammar has one level, so it accepts a * b + c as a * (b + c) — the operator order in the input determines the tree, not the operators' precedences. A stratified grammar E_n := E_{n-1} \mid E_{n-1}\, op_n\, E_n per level would fix this, with the parser becoming either a finite tuple of Löb-fixed mutually recursive parsers or a single parser whose state is a level index.

Left-associative operators. The current parser is single-pass right-associative because the recursion shape is [atom, op] · rhs. Left-associativity needs iteration with an accumulator, i.e. the loop body consumes one op · atom step on a left context that grows by accumulation. In the Löb-induction fixpoint shape, this is the runtime-prefix scenario discussed above: either an ad-hoc ▷-app-NE use or a different fixpoint, e.g. fixPr (right-handed) so that the recursive call consumes the final atom and the head accumulator is the runtime-shaped prefix.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Pratt's classical single parser with an explicit minPrec parameter unifies both: at each step it consumes one op only if \mathit {lbp}(\mathit {op}) > \mathit {minPrec}, and recurses with \mathit {rbp}(\mathit {op}) (which equals \mathit {lbp} for left-assoc, \mathit {lbp}-1 for right-assoc). Encoding this in our setting wants a Löb fix on the precedence-indexed family \triangleright (\forall p.\, \mathsf {Parser}\,E) \vdash \forall p.\, \mathsf {Parser}\,E. The static-prefix restriction is no longer the obstacle — the open question is the cleanest way to thread the runtime precedence through the recursive call. Punted to a follow-up.
